items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A long, coiled molecule of DNA (with proteins) found in the nucleus that carries many genes"?
items.answer: chromosome
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of chromosome.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a nucleotide and DNA.
items.answer: A nucleotide is a single unit (phosphate, sugar, base); DNA is the long polymer of millions of nucleotides in two strands.
items.markingKey: A nucleotide is a single unit (phosphate, sugar, base); DNA is the long polymer of millions of nucleotides in two strands. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "Only some of your body cells contain DNA for eye colour." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Almost every body cell (except mature red blood cells) contains the full genome; genes are switched on or off in different cells.
items.markingKey: Almost every body cell (except mature red blood cells) contains the full genome; genes are switched on or off in different cells. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Analysis of DNA from a strain of E. coli shows that 20% of the bases are cytosine. Calculate the percentage of adenine.
items.markingKey: cytosine pairs with guanine, so guanine = 20% (M1); adenine + thymine = 100 − 40 = 60% (M1); each = 30% (A1).

items.stem:
Alessia extracted DNA from 50 g samples of strawberries using different volumes of washing-up liquid and weighed the DNA collected.

Volume of washing-up liquid / cm³ | Mass of DNA / g: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
2 | 0.24 | 0.23 | 0.23
4 | 0.34 | 0.33 | 0.33
6 | 0.39 | 0.39 | 0.37
8 | 0.43 | 0.41 | 0.41
10 | 0.44 | 0.43 | 0.43

Describe the trend shown by the results and explain it using scientific knowledge.
items.answer: The mass of DNA increases with the volume of detergent but levels off above about 6-8 cm³. Detergent breaks down the lipid cell and nuclear membranes, releasing DNA; once all the membranes are broken, extra detergent releases no more DNA.
items.markingKey: 1 trend: The mass of DNA increases with the volume of detergent but levels off above about 6-8 cm³.; 1 use of data (quote means/values); 1-2 explanation: Detergent breaks down the lipid cell and nuclear membranes, releasing DNA; once all the membranes are broken, extra detergent releases no more DNA.

items.stem: Write a risk assessment for an investigation into how the volume of washing-up liquid added affects the mass of DNA extracted from 50 g of strawberries. Identify two hazards, the risk each poses and how each risk will be reduced, and explain one ethical or environmental consideration.
items.answer: Key hazard(s): ethanol is highly flammable – no naked flames; wear eye protection. For each hazard: state what could go wrong, how likely/serious it is, and the precaution. Ethical/environmental: e.g. minimise waste and dispose of chemicals correctly, treat living organisms and volunteers with respect and consent.
items.markingKey: 2 two relevant hazards with the risk explained (e.g. ethanol is highly flammable – no naked flames; wear eye protection); 2 a specific precaution for each; 1 relevant ethical or environmental consideration.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Deoxyribonucleic acid: a double-helix polymer of nucleotides that carries the genetic code"?
items.answer: DNA
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of DNA.

items.stem: Explain why complementary base pairing allows DNA to be copied accurately.
items.answer: When the strands separate, each acts as a template; free nucleotides can only pair A–T and C–G, so each new strand is an exact complement and the two new molecules are identical to the original.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: When the strands separate, each acts as a template; free nucleotides can only pair A–T and C–G, so each new strand is an exact complement and the two new molecules are identical to the original. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims that in DNA, adenine pairs with cytosine because both are large bases. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Adenine pairs with thymine and cytosine with guanine; a large purine always pairs with a smaller pyrimidine, keeping the helix the same width.
items.markingKey: Adenine pairs with thymine and cytosine with guanine; a large purine always pairs with a smaller pyrimidine, keeping the helix the same width. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Jonas writes: "Genes are made of chromosomes." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: It is the other way round: chromosomes are made of DNA, and genes are short sections of that DNA.
items.markingKey: It is the other way round: chromosomes are made of DNA, and genes are short sections of that DNA. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Outline how the structure of DNA makes it suitable for storing and copying genetic information.
items.answer: Long molecule – stores a huge amount of information as a base sequence; double-stranded with complementary bases – each strand is a template for copying; weak hydrogen bonds – strands separate easily; sugar-phosphate backbone – strong and stable; coiled into chromosomes – fits in the nucleus.
items.markingKey: Long molecule – stores a huge amount of information as a base sequence; double-stranded with complementary bases – each strand is a template for copying; weak hydrogen bonds – strands separate easily; sugar-phosphate backbone – strong and stable; coiled into chromosomes – fits in the nucleus.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "cytokinesis"?
options: The entire genetic material of an organism
The longest stage of the cell cycle, in which the cell grows, makes new organelles and replicates its DNA
The sequence of growth, DNA replication and division that a cell goes through: interphase, mitosis and cytokinesis
The division of the cytoplasm to form two separate daughter cells after the nucleus has divided
items.answer: The division of the cytoplasm to form two separate daughter cells after the nucleus has divided
items.markingKey: D. "cytokinesis" is the division of the cytoplasm to form two separate daughter cells after the nucleus has divided.

items.stem: Explain why DNA must be replicated before a cell divides by mitosis.
items.answer: Each daughter cell must receive a full, identical set of chromosomes; copying the DNA first means there are two chromatids per chromosome, one for each new cell.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Each daughter cell must receive a full, identical set of chromosomes; copying the DNA first means there are two chromatids per chromosome, one for each new cell. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "In mitosis the chromosome number halves so the daughter cells are smaller." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Mitosis keeps the chromosome number the same (46 → 46); halving happens in meiosis.
items.markingKey: Mitosis keeps the chromosome number the same (46 → 46); halving happens in meiosis. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: In an investigation into how the distance from the root tip affects the mitotic index of onion root cells, state the dependent variable and describe how Felix should measure it.
items.answer: mitotic index – number of cells in mitosis ÷ total cells counted in a field of view at ×400
items.markingKey: 1 mark for naming the dependent variable, 1 mark for a valid measuring method/instrument with unit: mitotic index – number of cells in mitosis ÷ total cells counted in a field of view at ×400.

items.stem: A culture of 10 plant callus cells divides by mitosis every 20 hours. Assuming every cell keeps dividing, how many cells will there be after 140 hours?
items.markingKey: M1 number of divisions = 140 ÷ 20 = 7; M1 cells = 10 × 2^7; A1 1280.

items.stem: Maya counted 200 cells in a squash of an onion root tip; 28 of them were in mitosis. The whole cell cycle takes 16 hours. Calculate the mitotic index and estimate how long, in minutes, mitosis lasts.
items.markingKey: M1 mitotic index = cells in mitosis ÷ total = 28/200 = 0.140; M1 time ∝ proportion: 0.140 × 16 h × 60; A1 134 min.

items.stem: Design a safe and valid method to investigate how the distance from the root tip affects the mitotic index of onion root cells. In your answer include the variables, the equipment, the range and number of values of the independent variable, the number of repeats, safety and how the data will be recorded and processed.
items.answer: Grow onion roots in water for 5 days at 20 °C; cut 2 mm sections at 0, 2, 4, 6, 8 mm from the tip; warm in 1 M HCl at 60 °C for 5 min, rinse, stain with toluidine blue and squash under a cover slip; count cells in mitosis and total cells in three fields of view at ×400; repeat with 3 roots and calculate mean mitotic index.
items.markingKey: MYP criterion B: 1 independent variable with at least 5 values in a sensible range; 1 dependent variable and how it is measured; 1 at least two controls and how they are controlled; 1 logical step-by-step procedure with equipment; 1 at least 3 repeats and calculation of a mean; 1 relevant safety point (hydrochloric acid is corrosive and stain can mark skin – wear eye protection and gloves; take care with scalpel). Model: Grow onion roots in water for 5 days at 20 °C; cut 2 mm sections at 0, 2, 4, 6, 8 mm from the tip; warm in 1 M HCl at 60 °C for 5 min, rinse, stain with toluidine blue and squash under a cover slip; count cells in mitosis and total cells in three fields of view at ×400; repeat with 3 roots and calculate mean mitotic index.

items.stem: Describe the main events of each stage of mitosis, in order, and explain how the process produces two genetically identical cells.
items.answer: Prophase: chromosomes condense, nuclear membrane breaks down, spindle forms. Metaphase: chromosomes line up at the equator. Anaphase: sister chromatids separate to opposite poles. Telophase: nuclear membranes re-form; cytokinesis divides the cell. Identical because DNA was copied exactly and each cell gets one chromatid of every chromosome.
items.markingKey: Prophase: chromosomes condense, nuclear membrane breaks down, spindle forms. Metaphase: chromosomes line up at the equator. Anaphase: sister chromatids separate to opposite poles. Telophase: nuclear membranes re-form; cytokinesis divides the cell. Identical because DNA was copied exactly and each cell gets one chromatid of every chromosome.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The sequence of growth, DNA replication and division that a cell goes through: interphase, mitosis and cytokinesis"?
items.answer: cell cycle
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of cell cycle.

items.stem: Explain why most of the cells seen in a root-tip squash are in interphase.
items.answer: Interphase is the longest stage of the cell cycle, so at any moment the largest proportion of cells is in it; the proportion of cells in a stage is proportional to the time spent in that stage.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Interphase is the longest stage of the cell cycle, so at any moment the largest proportion of cells is in it; the proportion of cells in a stage is proportional to the time spent in that stage. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between mitosis and cytokinesis.
items.answer: Mitosis is the division of the nucleus; cytokinesis is the division of the cytoplasm that follows.
items.markingKey: Mitosis is the division of the nucleus; cytokinesis is the division of the cytoplasm that follows. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Mei grew garlic roots at different temperatures and counted the number of cells in mitosis in a field of view of 100 cells.

Temperature / °C | Cells in mitosis / cells per 100: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
5 | 5 | 5 | 5
10 | 8 | 8 | 8
15 | 11 | 11 | 11
20 | 14 | 14 | 15
25 | 18 | 18 | 17

State the temperature at which the repeat readings are least consistent, and calculate the range of the readings at that value. Suggest one way to make the data more reliable.
items.answer: 20 °C; range = 1 cells per 100; e.g. take more repeats and discard anomalies / use more precise apparatus
items.markingKey: 1 20 °C; 1 range = max − min = 15 − 14 = 1 cells per 100; 1 valid improvement (more repeats, more precise instrument, control a named variable).

items.stem: Briefly describe healing of a grazed knee and explain what it reveals about the role of mitosis in repair.
items.answer: Cells in the basal layer of the epidermis divide repeatedly to replace damaged cells over several days. Mitosis produces new, genetically identical skin cells that replace the lost ones.
items.markingKey: Context (Cells in the basal layer of the epidermis divide repeatedly to replace damaged cells over several days.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Mitosis produces new, genetically identical skin cells that replace the lost ones. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the role of mitosis in repair.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of the view that the story of the HeLa cells shows that patients should always give consent before their cells are used in research.
items.answer: Informed consent is now an accepted ethical principle; the HeLa case shows why, even though the research brought huge benefits.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: respect for autonomy and the family’s right to know; companies profited without the family benefiting. Arguments against: in 1951 consent rules did not exist and the research saved millions of lives; anonymised samples may be needed for large studies. Supported judgement: Informed consent is now an accepted ethical principle; the HeLa case shows why, even though the research brought huge benefits.

items.stem: Which process restores the diploid number after meiosis?
items.answer: Fertilisation
items.markingKey: B. Two haploid gametes fuse to give a diploid zygote.

items.stem: Explain how meiosis produces genetic variation.
items.answer: Independent assortment: homologous pairs line up randomly, so each gamete gets a different mix of maternal and paternal chromosomes; crossing over swaps sections between homologous chromosomes, creating new allele combinations.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Independent assortment: homologous pairs line up randomly, so each gamete gets a different mix of maternal and paternal chromosomes; crossing over swaps sections between homologous chromosomes, creating new allele combinations. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between haploid and diploid.
items.answer: Haploid cells have one set of chromosomes (n = 23 in humans); diploid cells have two sets (2n = 46).
items.markingKey: Haploid cells have one set of chromosomes (n = 23 in humans); diploid cells have two sets (2n = 46). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Tariq is investigating whether pea plants grown from seed (sexual reproduction) show more variation in height than plants grown from cuttings of one parent (asexual reproduction). Formulate a testable hypothesis and justify it using scientific knowledge.
items.answer: If plants are grown from seed, then their heights will vary more than plants from cuttings, because meiosis and fertilisation produce genetically different offspring, whereas cuttings are clones from mitosis.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: testable prediction in "if … then …" form linking the independent and dependent variables; 1-2 marks: scientific explanation. Model: If plants are grown from seed, then their heights will vary more than plants from cuttings, because meiosis and fertilisation produce genetically different offspring, whereas cuttings are clones from mitosis.

items.stem: A student claims that a human egg cell has 46 chromosomes because it will become a baby. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: An egg is haploid with 23 chromosomes; the zygote gets 46 after fertilisation with a 23-chromosome sperm.
items.markingKey: An egg is haploid with 23 chromosomes; the zygote gets 46 after fertilisation with a 23-chromosome sperm. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student claims that identical twins are genetically identical because they came from two eggs fertilised at the same time. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Identical twins form when one zygote splits into two embryos; twins from two eggs are non-identical.
items.markingKey: Identical twins form when one zygote splits into two embryos; twins from two eggs are non-identical. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Compare mitosis and meiosis in a table covering: number of divisions, number of daughter cells, chromosome number of daughter cells, genetic similarity, and where each occurs in humans. Then explain why both processes are needed in the life cycle of a human.
items.answer: Mitosis: 1 division, 2 cells, diploid (46), identical, body tissues. Meiosis: 2 divisions, 4 cells, haploid (23), genetically different, testes/ovaries. Meiosis makes gametes so fertilisation restores 46; mitosis then grows the zygote into a body of identical cells and repairs tissue.
items.markingKey: Mitosis: 1 division, 2 cells, diploid (46), identical, body tissues. Meiosis: 2 divisions, 4 cells, haploid (23), genetically different, testes/ovaries. Meiosis makes gametes so fertilisation restores 46; mitosis then grows the zygote into a body of identical cells and repairs tissue.

items.stem: Alessia investigated whether pea plants grown from seed (sexual reproduction) show more variation in height than plants grown from cuttings of one parent (asexual reproduction). The method had this weakness: only five plants of each type were measured. Evaluate how this weakness affects the validity of the results and suggest an improvement to the method.
items.answer: measure at least 30 plants of each type so the spread is representative and anomalies have less effect
items.markingKey: 1 identifies how the weakness introduces error or an uncontrolled variable; 1 states the effect on the results/conclusion; 1-2 a specific, practical improvement: measure at least 30 plants of each type so the spread is representative and anomalies have less effect

items.stem: How many cells are produced when one cell divides by meiosis?
items.answer: Four
items.markingKey: B. Meiosis has two divisions, producing four haploid cells.

items.stem: Distinguish between meiosis and mitosis.
items.answer: Mitosis: one division, two diploid daughter cells, genetically identical, for growth and repair. Meiosis: two divisions, four haploid cells, genetically different, for making gametes.
items.markingKey: Mitosis: one division, two diploid daughter cells, genetically identical, for growth and repair. Meiosis: two divisions, four haploid cells, genetically different, for making gametes. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why sexual reproduction produces more variation than asexual reproduction.
items.answer: Sexual reproduction uses meiosis (independent assortment, crossing over) and random fertilisation between two parents; asexual reproduction uses mitosis, producing genetically identical clones.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Sexual reproduction uses meiosis (independent assortment, crossing over) and random fertilisation between two parents; asexual reproduction uses mitosis, producing genetically identical clones. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims that meiosis produces two identical cells, just like mitosis but in the sex organs. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Meiosis produces four cells, each haploid and genetically different.
items.markingKey: Meiosis produces four cells, each haploid and genetically different. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: The body cells of a house mouse contain 40 chromosomes. State the number of chromosomes in (a) a gamete, (b) a zygote, (c) a cell produced by mitosis.
items.markingKey: (a) haploid = 40/2 = 20 (1); (b) gametes fuse: 20 + 20 = 40 (1); (c) mitosis keeps the number: 40 (1).

items.stem: To what extent is it true that sexual reproduction is always better for a species than asexual reproduction?
items.answer: Neither is always better; many organisms (strawberries, aphids) use both depending on conditions.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: variation lets some individuals survive changes such as new diseases; allows natural selection and adaptation. Arguments against: needs two parents and time and energy to find a mate; good allele combinations can be broken up; asexual reproduction is fast and suits a stable environment (e.g. aphids, potatoes). Supported judgement: Neither is always better; many organisms (strawberries, aphids) use both depending on conditions. Markbands (8 marks): MYP criterion D (0-8, scaled): 7-8 explains thoroughly how the science is applied to address the issue, discusses and evaluates the implications (moral, ethical, social, economic, political, cultural or environmental), and documents sources consistently; 5-6 explains and discusses; 3-4 outlines; 1-2 states.

items.stem: Which disease has been treated by bone marrow transplants for decades?
items.answer: Leukaemia
items.markingKey: C. Bone marrow stem cells replace the patient’s blood-forming cells.

items.stem: Distinguish between an adult stem cell and an embryonic stem cell.
items.answer: Embryonic stem cells come from early embryos and can form almost any cell type; adult stem cells are found in some tissues (e.g. bone marrow) and form only a limited range.
items.markingKey: Embryonic stem cells come from early embryos and can form almost any cell type; adult stem cells are found in some tissues (e.g. bone marrow) and form only a limited range. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why gardeners can grow a whole new plant from a small cutting.
items.answer: Meristem cells in the cutting are undifferentiated and can divide by mitosis and differentiate into all the tissues of a new plant, which is a clone of the parent. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Meristem cells in the cutting are undifferentiated and can divide by mitosis and differentiate into all the tissues of a new plant, which is a clone of the parent. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: In an investigation into how the length of a cauliflower explant affects the number of new shoots that grow from it in tissue culture, state the dependent variable and describe how Tariq should measure it.
items.answer: number of new shoots counted after 4 weeks
items.markingKey: 1 mark for naming the dependent variable, 1 mark for a valid measuring method/instrument with unit: number of new shoots counted after 4 weeks.

items.stem: Sofia writes: "Animal cells can differentiate throughout life just like plant cells." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Most animal cells differentiate early and lose this ability; plant meristem cells can differentiate throughout life.
items.markingKey: Most animal cells differentiate early and lose this ability; plant meristem cells can differentiate throughout life. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Nia plans an investigation into how the length of a cauliflower explant affects the number of new shoots that grow from it in tissue culture. Describe how the results should be recorded, processed and presented, and explain how the reliability and validity of the conclusion will be judged.
items.answer: Results table with the independent variable (length of explant (mm)) in the first column and repeat readings of the dependent variable with units in headings; calculate means (ignoring anomalies); plot a suitable graph of the mean dependent variable against the independent variable with a line of best fit; describe the trend and compare with the hypothesis; judge reliability from the spread of repeats and validity from how well variables were controlled.
items.markingKey: 1 table with IV, repeats and units; 1 means calculated, anomalies identified and excluded; 1 appropriate graph (line graph/scatter for continuous IV, bar chart for categorical) with line of best fit; 1 trend compared with hypothesis; 1 reliability (spread of repeats) and validity (controls) discussed.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "embryonic stem cell"?
options: A stem cell from an early embryo that can differentiate into almost any cell type (pluripotent)
The longest stage of the cell cycle, in which the cell grows, makes new organelles and replicates its DNA
The fusion of a male and a female gamete nucleus to form a diploid zygote
An undifferentiated cell that can divide repeatedly and differentiate into different types of specialised cell
items.answer: A stem cell from an early embryo that can differentiate into almost any cell type (pluripotent)
items.markingKey: A. "embryonic stem cell" is a stem cell from an early embryo that can differentiate into almost any cell type (pluripotent).

items.stem: Explain the difference between a stem cell and a specialised cell.
items.answer: A stem cell is undifferentiated and can divide and become different cell types; a specialised cell has differentiated, has a structure for one function and usually divides rarely.
items.markingKey: A stem cell is undifferentiated and can divide and become different cell types; a specialised cell has differentiated, has a structure for one function and usually divides rarely. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims that animal cells can differentiate throughout life just like plant cells. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Most animal cells differentiate early and lose this ability; plant meristem cells can differentiate throughout life.
items.markingKey: Most animal cells differentiate early and lose this ability; plant meristem cells can differentiate throughout life. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Using tissue culture of orchids and bananas as an example, explain plant stem cells and cloning.
items.answer: Growers take tiny pieces of meristem and grow thousands of identical plants on sterile agar with plant hormones. Meristem cells divide by mitosis and differentiate into whole plants that are clones of the parent.
items.markingKey: Context (Growers take tiny pieces of meristem and grow thousands of identical plants on sterile agar with plant hormones.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Meristem cells divide by mitosis and differentiate into whole plants that are clones of the parent. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to plant stem cells and cloning.

items.stem: "Research using human embryonic stem cells should be allowed." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Many countries allow it under strict regulation (e.g. up to 14 days, licensed labs); the judgement depends on beliefs about the moral status of the embryo, balanced against potential cures.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: could treat diseases such as type 1 diabetes, Parkinson’s and spinal injury; embryos used are often spare ones from IVF that would be destroyed. Arguments against: some people believe an embryo has a right to life from conception; risk of transplanted cells forming tumours or being contaminated; iPS cells may give similar benefits without embryos. Supported judgement: Many countries allow it under strict regulation (e.g. up to 14 days, licensed labs); the judgement depends on beliefs about the moral status of the embryo, balanced against potential cures. Markbands (15 marks): MYP criterion D (0-8, scaled): 7-8 explains thoroughly how the science is applied to address the issue, discusses and evaluates the implications (moral, ethical, social, economic, political, cultural or environmental), and documents sources consistently; 5-6 explains and discusses; 3-4 outlines; 1-2 states.

items.stem: In which stage of mitosis do chromosomes line up along the equator of the cell?
items.answer: Metaphase
items.markingKey: D. In metaphase spindle fibres attach to centromeres and align the chromosomes at the equator.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "fertilisation"?
options: The entire genetic material of an organism
The fusion of a male and a female gamete nucleus to form a diploid zygote
The rule that adenine always pairs with thymine and cytosine always pairs with guanine across the two DNA strands
A region of undifferentiated, dividing cells in plants, found at root and shoot tips
items.answer: The fusion of a male and a female gamete nucleus to form a diploid zygote
items.markingKey: B. "fertilisation" is the fusion of a male and a female gamete nucleus to form a diploid zygote.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "complementary base pairing".
items.answer: The rule that adenine always pairs with thymine and cytosine always pairs with guanine across the two DNA strands
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the rule that adenine always pairs with thymine and cytosine always pairs with guanine across the two DNA strands. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain the difference between an adult stem cell and an embryonic stem cell.
items.answer: Embryonic stem cells come from early embryos and can form almost any cell type; adult stem cells are found in some tissues (e.g. bone marrow) and form only a limited range.
items.markingKey: Embryonic stem cells come from early embryos and can form almost any cell type; adult stem cells are found in some tissues (e.g. bone marrow) and form only a limited range. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why cancer can develop when the control of the cell cycle fails.
items.answer: Mutations in genes that control the cycle let a cell divide by mitosis repeatedly without stopping, forming a tumour; malignant tumours can invade tissues and spread.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Mutations in genes that control the cycle let a cell divide by mitosis repeatedly without stopping, forming a tumour; malignant tumours can invade tissues and spread. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Mateo writes: "Identical twins are genetically identical because they came from two eggs fertilised at the same time." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Identical twins form when one zygote splits into two embryos; twins from two eggs are non-identical.
items.markingKey: Identical twins form when one zygote splits into two embryos; twins from two eggs are non-identical. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why the amount of adenine in a DNA molecule equals the amount of thymine.
items.answer: Every adenine on one strand is paired with a thymine on the other strand, so the numbers must be equal (Chargaff’s rule).
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Every adenine on one strand is paired with a thymine on the other strand, so the numbers must be equal (Chargaff’s rule). (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain why embryonic stem cells are considered more useful in research than adult stem cells.
items.answer: Embryonic stem cells are pluripotent – they can become almost any cell type – whereas adult stem cells can usually only form a few related types (e.g. blood cells).
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Embryonic stem cells are pluripotent – they can become almost any cell type – whereas adult stem cells can usually only form a few related types (e.g. blood cells). (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "Mitosis produces genetic variation between daughter cells." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Mitosis produces genetically identical cells (clones); variation comes from meiosis and fertilisation.
items.markingKey: Mitosis produces genetically identical cells (clones); variation comes from meiosis and fertilisation. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly describe wheat breeding by Norman Borlaug in Mexico and explain what it reveals about genetic variation from sexual reproduction.
items.answer: Crossing many wheat varieties produced offspring with new combinations of disease resistance and short stems, raising yields worldwide. Meiosis and fertilisation shuffled alleles from different parents, giving new combinations to select from.
items.markingKey: Context (Crossing many wheat varieties produced offspring with new combinations of disease resistance and short stems, raising yields worldwide.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Meiosis and fertilisation shuffled alleles from different parents, giving new combinations to select from. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to genetic variation from sexual reproduction.

items.stem: Omar plans to investigate how the volume of washing-up liquid added affects the mass of DNA extracted from 50 g of strawberries. State three variables that must be controlled to make this a fair test.
items.answer: Any three of: mass of strawberries; volume and temperature of ice-cold ethanol; salt concentration; mashing time
items.markingKey: 1 mark each, max 3: mass of strawberries – more fruit gives more cells and more DNA; volume and temperature of ice-cold ethanol – ethanol temperature affects how much DNA precipitates; salt concentration – salt helps DNA clump together; mashing time – more mashing breaks open more cells. The independent or dependent variable scores 0.

items.stem: Briefly describe tissue culture of orchids and bananas and explain what it reveals about plant stem cells and cloning.
items.answer: Growers take tiny pieces of meristem and grow thousands of identical plants on sterile agar with plant hormones. Meristem cells divide by mitosis and differentiate into whole plants that are clones of the parent.
items.markingKey: Context (Growers take tiny pieces of meristem and grow thousands of identical plants on sterile agar with plant hormones.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Meristem cells divide by mitosis and differentiate into whole plants that are clones of the parent. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to plant stem cells and cloning.

items.stem:
Freya grew garlic roots at different temperatures and counted the number of cells in mitosis in a field of view of 100 cells.

Temperature / °C | Cells in mitosis / cells per 100: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
5 | 5 | 5 | 5
10 | 8 | 8 | 8
15 | 12 | 11 | 12
20 | 15 | 15 | 16
25 | 18 | 18 | 18

State the temperature at which the repeat readings are least consistent, and calculate the range of the readings at that value. Suggest one way to make the data more reliable.
items.answer: 15 °C; range = 1 cells per 100; e.g. take more repeats and discard anomalies / use more precise apparatus
items.markingKey: 1 15 °C; 1 range = max − min = 12 − 11 = 1 cells per 100; 1 valid improvement (more repeats, more precise instrument, control a named variable).

items.stem:
Amara took cuttings from one parent pea plant, so all the plants were clones produced by mitosis. The clones were grown with different fertiliser concentrations and measured their height after 6 weeks.

Fertiliser concentration / g/dm³ | Plant height / cm: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
0 | 17.0 | 16.7 | 16.4
1 | 20.0 | 21.6 | 20.6
2 | 23.7 | 24.8 | 23.6
3 | 27.9 | 28.0 | 27.7
4 | 32.2 | 31.4 | 31.8

Describe the trend shown by the results and explain it using scientific knowledge.
items.answer: Mean plant height increases as fertiliser concentration increases. The clones are genetically identical, so the differences are environmental: fertiliser supplies mineral ions such as nitrate for making proteins, so cells divide and grow more.
items.markingKey: 1 trend: Mean plant height increases as fertiliser concentration increases.; 1 use of data (quote means/values); 1-2 explanation: The clones are genetically identical, so the differences are environmental: fertiliser supplies mineral ions such as nitrate for making proteins, so cells divide and grow more.

items.stem: A student claims that only some of your body cells contain DNA for eye colour. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Almost every body cell (except mature red blood cells) contains the full genome; genes are switched on or off in different cells.
items.markingKey: Almost every body cell (except mature red blood cells) contains the full genome; genes are switched on or off in different cells. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "Specialised cells have lost the genes they do not use." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: They keep all their genes; unused genes are switched off, not removed.
items.markingKey: They keep all their genes; unused genes are switched off, not removed. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Chemotherapy drugs that stop mitosis are the best treatment for cancer."
items.answer: Chemotherapy is effective but not always best; the choice depends on the type and stage of cancer, often in combination with other treatments.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: they kill rapidly dividing cancer cells throughout the body, including cells that have spread; they can shrink tumours before surgery. Arguments against: they also damage healthy dividing cells (hair follicles, gut lining, bone marrow), causing side effects; cancer cells can become resistant; surgery, radiotherapy or targeted immunotherapy may work better for some cancers. Supported judgement: Chemotherapy is effective but not always best; the choice depends on the type and stage of cancer, often in combination with other treatments.

items.stem: "Sexual reproduction is always better for a species than asexual reproduction." Discuss.
items.answer: Neither is always better; many organisms (strawberries, aphids) use both depending on conditions.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: variation lets some individuals survive changes such as new diseases; allows natural selection and adaptation. Arguments against: needs two parents and time and energy to find a mate; good allele combinations can be broken up; asexual reproduction is fast and suits a stable environment (e.g. aphids, potatoes). Supported judgement: Neither is always better; many organisms (strawberries, aphids) use both depending on conditions. Markbands (8 marks): MYP criterion D (0-8, scaled): 7-8 explains thoroughly how the science is applied to address the issue, discusses and evaluates the implications (moral, ethical, social, economic, political, cultural or environmental), and documents sources consistently; 5-6 explains and discusses; 3-4 outlines; 1-2 states.

items.stem: To what extent is it true that personal genome testing kits sold directly to the public do more good than harm?
items.answer: The benefit depends on regulation: with privacy protection and access to counselling, benefits can outweigh harms; without them the risks are significant.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: they can reveal carrier status or risk of conditions so people can make health choices; they encourage interest in science and family history. Arguments against: results are probabilistic and may cause anxiety or false reassurance; genetic data privacy: companies may share data with insurers or police; no genetic counsellor to explain results. Supported judgement: The benefit depends on regulation: with privacy protection and access to counselling, benefits can outweigh harms; without them the risks are significant. Markbands (8 marks): MYP criterion D (0-8, scaled): 7-8 explains thoroughly how the science is applied to address the issue, discusses and evaluates the implications (moral, ethical, social, economic, political, cultural or environmental), and documents sources consistently; 5-6 explains and discusses; 3-4 outlines; 1-2 states.

items.stem: Outline how stem cells could be used to treat type 1 diabetes and evaluate two problems that must be solved first.
items.answer: Stem cells are grown and treated so they differentiate into insulin-secreting beta cells, then transplanted into the pancreas/liver. Problems: rejection by the immune system (and in type 1 diabetes the body attacks beta cells again); risk of uncontrolled division forming tumours; ethical issues if embryos used; cost.
items.markingKey: Stem cells are grown and treated so they differentiate into insulin-secreting beta cells, then transplanted into the pancreas/liver. Problems: rejection by the immune system (and in type 1 diabetes the body attacks beta cells again); risk of uncontrolled division forming tumours; ethical issues if embryos used; cost.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A mass of cells formed by uncontrolled mitosis"?
items.answer: tumour
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of tumour.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "meiosis"?
options: Deoxyribonucleic acid: a double-helix polymer of nucleotides that carries the genetic code
A type of cell division that produces four genetically different haploid cells (gametes) from one diploid cell
The sequence of growth, DNA replication and division that a cell goes through: interphase, mitosis and cytokinesis
The longest stage of the cell cycle, in which the cell grows, makes new organelles and replicates its DNA
items.answer: A type of cell division that produces four genetically different haploid cells (gametes) from one diploid cell
items.markingKey: B. "meiosis" is a type of cell division that produces four genetically different haploid cells (gametes) from one diploid cell.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A section of DNA on a chromosome that codes for a specific protein"?
items.answer: gene
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of gene.

items.stem: Distinguish between an embryonic stem cell and an adult stem cell.
items.answer: Embryonic stem cells come from early embryos and can form almost any cell type; adult stem cells are found in some tissues (e.g. bone marrow) and form only a limited range.
items.markingKey: Embryonic stem cells come from early embryos and can form almost any cell type; adult stem cells are found in some tissues (e.g. bone marrow) and form only a limited range. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Rafael writes: "Cells are resting during interphase because they are not dividing." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Interphase is very active: the cell grows, makes proteins and organelles and replicates its DNA.
items.markingKey: Interphase is very active: the cell grows, makes proteins and organelles and replicates its DNA. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between diploid and haploid.
items.answer: Haploid cells have one set of chromosomes (n = 23 in humans); diploid cells have two sets (2n = 46).
items.markingKey: Haploid cells have one set of chromosomes (n = 23 in humans); diploid cells have two sets (2n = 46). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between DNA and a nucleotide.
items.answer: A nucleotide is a single unit (phosphate, sugar, base); DNA is the long polymer of millions of nucleotides in two strands.
items.markingKey: A nucleotide is a single unit (phosphate, sugar, base); DNA is the long polymer of millions of nucleotides in two strands. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between a specialised cell and a stem cell.
items.answer: A stem cell is undifferentiated and can divide and become different cell types; a specialised cell has differentiated, has a structure for one function and usually divides rarely.
items.markingKey: A stem cell is undifferentiated and can divide and become different cell types; a specialised cell has differentiated, has a structure for one function and usually divides rarely. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between cytokinesis and mitosis.
items.answer: Mitosis is the division of the nucleus; cytokinesis is the division of the cytoplasm that follows.
items.markingKey: Mitosis is the division of the nucleus; cytokinesis is the division of the cytoplasm that follows. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "Identical twins are genetically identical because they came from two eggs fertilised at the same time." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Identical twins form when one zygote splits into two embryos; twins from two eggs are non-identical.
items.markingKey: Identical twins form when one zygote splits into two embryos; twins from two eggs are non-identical. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: One strand of a section of DNA has the base sequence ACCGGCCCAGTC. Write the base sequence of the complementary strand.
items.answer: TGGCCGGGTCAG
items.markingKey: A↔T and C↔G applied to every base: TGGCCGGGTCAG (1-2 marks; −1 per error).

items.stem:
Kwame grew cauliflower tissue-culture explants on agar containing different concentrations of plant hormone and measured the number of shoots formed after 4 weeks.

Hormone concentration / mg/dm³ | Number of shoots / shoots per explant: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
0.0 | 2 | 2 | 2
0.5 | 5 | 4 | 5
1.0 | 5 | 7 | 7
1.5 | 9 | 10 | 10
2.0 | 12 | 12 | 12

Identify the anomalous result. Calculate the mean number of shoots at 1.0 mg/dm³, excluding the anomaly.
items.answer: Anomaly: 5 shoots per explant (trial 1 at 1.0 mg/dm³); mean = 7.0 shoots per explant
items.markingKey: 1 anomaly identified (5) as it does not fit the pattern of the other repeats; M1 mean of the two remaining values; A1 7.0 shoots per explant.

items.stem: Using HeLa cells, taken from Henrietta Lacks in 1951 as an example, explain uncontrolled mitosis in cancer cells.
items.answer: Cancer cells from her cervical tumour kept dividing indefinitely in culture and have been used in research on polio vaccines and cancer. They divide without the normal limits of the cell cycle, showing what happens when control of mitosis is lost; the case also raised issues of consent.
items.markingKey: Context (Cancer cells from her cervical tumour kept dividing indefinitely in culture and have been used in research on polio vaccines and cancer.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: They divide without the normal limits of the cell cycle, showing what happens when control of mitosis is lost; the case also raised issues of consent. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to uncontrolled mitosis in cancer cells.

items.stem: The body cells of a fruit fly (Drosophila) contain 8 chromosomes. State the number of chromosomes in (a) a gamete, (b) a zygote, (c) a cell produced by mitosis.
items.markingKey: (a) haploid = 8/2 = 4 (1); (b) gametes fuse: 4 + 4 = 8 (1); (c) mitosis keeps the number: 8 (1).

items.stem: "Genes are made of chromosomes." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: It is the other way round: chromosomes are made of DNA, and genes are short sections of that DNA.
items.markingKey: It is the other way round: chromosomes are made of DNA, and genes are short sections of that DNA. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Felix writes: "Stem cells can only be found in embryos." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Adults have stem cells too, e.g. in bone marrow, skin and the gut lining, though they form a narrower range of cells.
items.markingKey: Adults have stem cells too, e.g. in bone marrow, skin and the gut lining, though they form a narrower range of cells. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against the view that the story of the HeLa cells shows that patients should always give consent before their cells are used in research.
items.answer: Informed consent is now an accepted ethical principle; the HeLa case shows why, even though the research brought huge benefits.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: respect for autonomy and the family’s right to know; companies profited without the family benefiting. Arguments against: in 1951 consent rules did not exist and the research saved millions of lives; anonymised samples may be needed for large studies. Supported judgement: Informed consent is now an accepted ethical principle; the HeLa case shows why, even though the research brought huge benefits.

items.stem: A species has a diploid number of 2n = 8. (a) State the number of chromosomes in a gamete. (b) Calculate the number of different combinations of chromosomes possible in the gametes from independent assortment alone. (c) Explain why the real number of genetically different gametes is even larger.
items.answer: (a) 4 (b) 2⁴ = 16 (c) crossing over creates new combinations of alleles within chromosomes.
items.markingKey: (a) 4 (b) 2⁴ = 16 (c) crossing over creates new combinations of alleles within chromosomes.

items.stem: A DNA sample contains 22% thymine. Calculate the percentage of each of the other three bases and explain your reasoning.
items.answer: A = 22% (pairs with T); A + T = 44%, so C + G = 56%; C = G = 28%.
items.markingKey: A = 22% (pairs with T); A + T = 44%, so C + G = 56%; C = G = 28%.

items.stem: "Unlicensed “stem cell clinics” that sell treatments to the public should be banned." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Strong regulation and clinical trials protect patients; unproven treatments should not be sold.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: treatments are often unproven and some patients have been harmed (e.g. blindness after eye injections); they exploit desperate patients for high fees. Arguments against: patients have a right to choose treatments; banning may push clinics to other countries. Supported judgement: Strong regulation and clinical trials protect patients; unproven treatments should not be sold.
